title: steady-throughput-validation-and-coldstart-profiling
body:
Purpose
This is a working playbook for validating steady throughput SLOs and isolating coldstart-related performance regressions in the serving runtime. Focus is on reproducible harness configs, a short warmup strategy that converges quickly, and a targeted coldstart profiling step that captures driver/kernel/host effects separate from steady-state bottlenecks.

Scope
- Applies to hosted and dedicated GPU-backed model variants (A100, H100, and 8-bit quantized variants).
- Covers throughput validation across a range of sequence lengths and prompt composition (short chat turns vs long context generation).
- Does NOT replace long-running soak tests; it is a lightweight harness for rapid iteration and root-cause triage.

Definitions
- Steady throughput: token/sec and request/sec when the runtime has reached stable KV cache and batching behavior and per-request latency variance is within an acceptable band.
- Coldstart: first N requests after a scale-up or model swap where JIT, kernel caching, or memory allocations produce measurably higher latency or lower throughput.
- Priming/warmup: controlled sequence of requests designed to bring runtime into steady state quickly and repeatably.

High-level methodology
1) Baseline collection: run a small calibration sweep to identify rough latency/throughput operating points for the model+hardware combination. Collect minimal signals for 3–5 mins.
2) Deterministic warmup: apply a fixed, reproducible warmup schedule (see recipe) that exercises model at target concurrency/batch shapes.
3) Steady probe: run fixed-duration steady-phase window (recommended 10m for labs, 30m for release candidate) collecting full telemetry.
4) Coldstart isolation: trigger a scale-up or model swap, then immediately run a short coldstart trace capturing first 60–120 requests at high sampling rate.
5) Post-analysis: decompose variance into categories (scheduling, memory, kernel jitter, network) and produce a concise regression summary.

Experiment matrix (recommended minimal set)
- Concurrency sweep: [1, 4, 8, 16] concurrent requests at target batch sizing.
- Seq len buckets: [32, 128, 1024] tokens.
- Batch shaping: fixed-batch (elastic batching disabled) vs continuous batching.
- Warmup durations: [30s, 90s, 3m].
- Coldstart triggers: container restart, model switch, scale-up node.

Loadgen config recipes
- Example loadgen pseudo-config (CLI-like)
  --model=redwood-opt-13b
  --concurrency=8
  --seq-len=128
  --qps=auto
  --batch-policy=continuous
  --duration=600s  # steady probe
  --warmup-policy=deterministic
  --warmup-sequence-file=warmup/seq-128-const.json
  --seed=42
  --report-interval=10s

- Important knobs to expose and lock in for repeatability:
  * seed (randomized jitter)
  * exact inter-arrival schedule (poisson vs fixed interval)
  * batch shaping toggles (elastic vs fixed)
  * client-side concurrency drivers (one driver per client thread)

Warmup/priming recipe (deterministic)
- Goal: reach steady-state in minimal time while avoiding artificial over-priming that masks production coldstarts.
- Heuristic warmup sequence (target concurrency C):
  1) 0–15s: ramp linearly from 1 to C/4 with short sequences (seq=32) at 0.5x target QPS.
  2) 15–45s: jump to C with seq=128 at 1.0x target QPS.
  3) 45–90s: sustain C concurrency with mixed seq samples (30% long 1024 tokens, 70% seq=128) at 0.9–1.1x QPS.
- Record per-request trace ids for first 200 requests after warmup for later correlation.

Coldstart profiling steps
1) Clear caches / simulate scale-up: whichever action replicates the customer-facing coldstart. For dedicated: rotate to a warm pool or create fresh replica.
2) Immediately start a high-frequency sampler for the first 120 requests (capture GPU activity counters, driver logs, kernel-load timings, malloc stats).
3) Collect host metrics at 1s resolution: CPU steal, page faults, hugepage allocations, PCIe errors, nvml counters (sm/temperature/power/engine activity).
4) Retain a binary-level trace (if available) for one coldstart run for offline disassembly of kernel loads.

Instrumentation and signals to collect
- Request-level: request_id, timestamp_recv, timestamp_start_compute, timestamp_end_compute, tokens_out, model_version, kv_cache_hit_rate.
- Host-level: cpu_user, cpu_system, cpu_steal, disk_iops, net_bytes, mem_rss, mem_gpu_free, page_faults.
- GPU-level: gpu_util, sm_efficiency, dram_util, pcie_rx, pcie_tx, power_watts, temperature_c.
- Runtime-level: batching_efficiency, avg_batch_size, queue_latency_ms, kernel_cache_misses, allocation_latency_ms.

Repeatability checklist (pre-run)
- [ ] Fixed seed set in loadgen and in any randomized prompt sampler.
- [ ] All drivers and runtime package versions pinned and noted in run metadata.
- [ ] No deployments, autoscaler events, or infra maintenance windows during runs.
- [ ] Background noise controlled: colocated noisy tenants disabled or migration planned.
- [ ] Time sync (NTP) validated across client and server nodes.
- [ ] Warmup sequence file checked in and referenced by commit SHA in metadata.

Quick analysis playbook
- Compute stable-window statistics: discard first X% of samples or first N seconds post warmup, then compute p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens/sec, and batch-size distribution.
- Use variance decomposition: attribute latency variance to (a) inter-arrival jitter, (b) queueing at dispatcher, (c) batch composition, (d) GPU kernel jitter.
- Plot sequential coldstart traces overlayed with steady-state median to visualize convergence time.
- Check GPU kernel load times vs kernel cache miss events; if kernel load correlates with first high-latency spikes, file a regression against driver/kernel packaging.

Common failure modes and heuristics
- Scenario: long tail only on first node after scale-up -> likely kernel/driver/hotplug. Mitigation: pre-load kernels during rolling upgrade.
- Scenario: throughput dip with unchanged latency distribution -> likely scheduling/backpressure; examine queue length and batch shaping.
- Scenario: GPU utilization low but latency high -> data-transfer/pcie bottleneck or host-side serialization. Capture pcie counters and host memcpy timings.

Reporting template (short)
- Run id: <timestamp>-<sha>
- Model / variant: redwood-opt-13b / q4_1
- Hardware: gcp-h100-8x / driver 535.54
- Warmup recipe: deterministic-90s-mixedseq-v1
- Steady window: 600s (discard first 60s)
- Steady tokens/sec: median=12.4k, p95=13.8k
- Coldstart 95th latency spike: +220ms over steady p95, converged after 36 requests
- Notes: kernel load observed on coldstart 2; filing JIRA-RT-4123

Open items / TODOs
- Automate microsecond-resolution kernel-load sampling in the harness (Rajiv)
- Add a synthetic workload that isolates PCIe vs GPU compute to confirm transfer bottlenecks (Sofia)
- Create a standardized warmup-file generator that takes a target distribution and emits deterministic sequences (Ethan)

Notes to self
- Keep the warmup short for CI (<=90s) but allow longer for release gating.
- Avoid over-fitting warmup to hide realistic coldstarts experienced in production edge cases.

References
- Internal: throughput playbooks, kernel packaging notes, driver upgrade checklist.
- External: vendor NVML docs, GPU performance counters cheat-sheets.

End of draft.
